docs.title: TradingEngine
docs.text: A low-latency algorithmic trading engine written in C++23, designed for direct exchange connectivity across multiple venues and protocols.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
TradingEngine is a multi-venue, multi-protocol order execution engine built for algorithmic trading. It handles the full lifecycle of an order — from market data ingestion and order book maintenance, through risk validation, to order construction and transmission to the exchange.

The engine is designed with a focus on predictable, low-latency execution. Every component on the hot path avoids dynamic allocation, uses lock-free data structures, and applies explicit cache-line isolation to minimize false sharing between threads.

Work in Progress

The engine is currently in its Core Performance Phase. The primary focus is achieving deterministic, low-latency execution on the "Happy Path." The following areas are under active development:

Strategy Engine – Implementation of the main decision-making logic is pending.

Database Integration – ClickHouse connectivity for post-trade analysis is partially implemented.

System Monitoring – A dedicated telemetry unit is planned to monitor pipeline health, thread-heartbeats, and latency histograms in real-time.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
The engine processes two concurrent pipelines:

Rx (Inbound) – Exchange → NetworkIO → Parser → OrderManager → RiskEngine

Tx (Outbound) – Strategy → RiskEngine → Builder → NetworkIO → Exchange

Each stage communicates via lock-free SPSC queues. Stages run on pinned CPU cores to eliminate scheduler interference.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• MarketBook — maintains aggregated best bid/ask per symbol using a B-tree price level structure. Publishes atomic best prices for consumption by the risk engine.
  • HashTables — custom hash tables for symbol lookup and exec ID dedup.

docs.title: Main
docs.text:
• NetworkIO — epoll-based non-blocking socket I/O. Manages TCP (FIX, OUCH) and UDP (ITCH) connections. Handles login/session lifecycle via SoupBinTCP.
  • Parser — protocol-specific parsers for FIX, OUCH, and ITCH. Dispatches parsed messages downstream.
  • OrderManager — maintains the internal order state. Matches execution reports against pending orders.
  • RiskEngine — dual-thread risk evaluation. One thread updates risk state from execution reports and market data; another validates outbound orders pre-trade.
  • Builder — constructs outbound protocol messages (FIX NewOrderSingle, OUCH Enter Order) from internal order structures.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
• SessionManager — tracks connection and login state per session.
  • LoginController — manages login sequences for SoupBinTCP and FIX sessions.
  • SoupBinTCP — SBT session layer handler (login, logout, heartbeat, sequencing).

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
• Builder_FIX / Builder_OUCH — venue and protocol-specific message serializers.
  • Parser_FIX / Parser_OUCH / Parser_ITCH — venue and protocol-specific message deserializers.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: • ClickhouseWriter — asynchronous trade and order event logging to ClickHouse (partially implemented).

docs.title: Design Highlights
docs.text:
• Zero-copy on hot path – Messages are written directly into preallocated packet buffers with no intermediate copies, eliminating heap allocation overhead during execution.

  • Lock-free pipeline – All inter-thread communication is handled via SPSC queues (boost::lockfree::spsc_queue). No mutexes or condition variables exist on production.

  • Atomic State & Memory Ordering – The pipeline utilizes std::atomic with explicit Memory Barriers (Acquire/Release semantics) for cross-thread synchronization. This ensures maximum throughput by avoiding expensive sequentially consistent (memory_order_seq_cst) operations where possible.

  • Cache-line isolation – Data structures are grouped by access pattern and isolated with alignas(64) to eliminate false sharing and optimize L1/L2 cache hits.

  • Code generation – ITCH/OUCH message types and symbol tables are strictly generated from exchange specifications at build time, ensuring binary-level accuracy.

  • Static Dispatch – The engine utilizes function pointer tables, switch-case, and tag dispatch to achieve high-performance routing while avoiding runtime vtable overhead.

  • Busy-Wait Polling – Network and Flow threads employ a 100% duty-cycle polling strategy. Spin-loops are optimized with _mm_pause() intrinsics to prevent CPU pipeline flushes and reduce power consumption while maintaining sub-microsecond responsiveness.

  • SIMD-Accelerated Parsing – The FIX parser utilizes SIMD intrinsics to batch-process tag/value delimiters, significantly reducing the clock cycles required for string-to-binary conversion.

  • Design Patterns – The engine applies several well-known design patterns across its pipeline. See Design Patterns for a detailed breakdown.

docs.title: Roadmap & Resilience Engineering
docs.text:
Current development ensures that the engine performs at peak speed when data is valid. The next phases will introduce robustness against "Real World" anomalies:

Phase 2: Production Readiness & Safety

  • Binary Journaling – Implementing a high-speed, sequential disk-logger to persist the last seen Sequence Numbers and critical state for instant recovery after crashes.

  • Validation & Boundary Checks – Adding Checksum validation and rigorous protection against malformed packets or protocol violations from the exchange side.

  • Secure Config Management – Transitioning from plain-text JSON credentials to AES-256 encrypted secrets with environment-based master keys.

  • Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL) – Integrating OpenSSL for FIX connectivity to ensure encrypted communication with exchange gateways.

Phase 3: Micro-Optimizations

  • Warm-up Sequences – Pre-market dummy-load injection to prime the Instruction Cache and Branch Predictor for "first-packet" stability.

  • Latency Telemetry – Integrating a non-intrusive monitoring unit to track nanosecond-level jitter across each pipeline stage without impacting the hot path.

docs.text: Architecture Diagram

docs.title: Architecture Decision
docs.text: Unified dispatch over per-protocol pipelines — Parser and builder dispatch units handle all protocol/venue combinations (FIX, OUCH BIST, OUCH NASDAQ, ITCH BIST, ITCH NASDAQ) within a single thread each. The target hardware has 10 cores / 16 threads; each main pipeline stage is pinned to a dedicated core, leaving no headroom for per-protocol pipelines under normal load. Per-protocol class boundaries are kept clean so splitting into independent pipelines later requires minimal structural change.

docs.title: Threading Model
docs.text:
Each component is pinned to a dedicated physical core with SCHED_FIFO to eliminate scheduling jitter.

Component Core Thread Policy Priority Network Rx/Tx P-core 1 Thread 0 SCHED_FIFO max Parser P-core 2 Thread 2 SCHED_FIFO max Order Manager P-core 3 Thread 4 SCHED_FIFO max Strategy P-core 4 Thread 6 SCHED_FIFO max Builder P-core 5 Thread 8 SCHED_FIFO max Risk Update P-core 6 Thread 10 SCHED_FIFO max Risk Check E-core 7 Thread 12 SCHED_FIFO max Database E-core 8 Thread 13 SCHED_FIFO max/2 Main E-core 9 Thread 14 SCHED OTHER default

docs.title: Network Design Decision
docs.text: Network Rx and Tx share a single thread on one P-core. Separating them would require dedicating an additional P-core to Tx — given the limited P-core count, the same loop handles both directions. E-cores were not considered for network due to their lower single-thread performance and cache characteristics.

docs.title: Risk Check Design Decision
docs.text: Risk Check is read-heavy — it validates positions and limits without mutating state. With P-cores fully allocated to latency-critical write path components, Risk Check was assigned to an E-core. Its read-only nature makes it tolerant of the lower single-thread throughput of E-cores.

docs.title: Design Patterns
docs.text: This page documents the design patterns applied across the TradingEngine pipeline. Each pattern is described briefly and mapped to its concrete usage in the codebase.

docs.title: Object Pool
docs.text:
What: Pre-allocate a fixed set of objects at startup and reuse them instead of allocating/deallocating on demand. Eliminates heap allocation on the hot path.

Where:

  1. ProtocolMessagePools — preallocated FIX/ITCH/OUCH message objects
  2. PacketPools — preallocated outbound and inbound network packet buffers
  3. OrderPool — preallocated order objects
  4. OrderRiskPool in RiskEngine — preallocated OrderRisk entries for active order tracking

Why: Dynamic allocation (new/delete) is non-deterministic in latency due to heap fragmentation and OS interaction. Object pools give O(1) predictable allocation with zero system calls on the hot path.

docs.title: Producer-Consumer (SPSC Queue)
docs.text:
What: Decouple producers and consumers of data using a shared queue. In this engine, all inter-thread communication uses lock-free Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) queues.

Where: Every pipeline stage boundary:

  1. receiver_to_parser — NetworkIO → ParserDispatch
  2. builder_to_sender — BuilderDispatch → NetworkIO
  3. parser_to_store — ParserDispatch → OrderManager
  4. store_to_risk — OrderManager → RiskEngine (update)
  5. strategy_to_risk — StrategyEngine → RiskEngine (check)
  6. risk_to_builder — RiskEngine → BuilderDispatch
  7. store_to_db — OrderManager → ClickhouseWriter
  8. db_to_parser — ClickhouseWriter → ParserDispatch

Why: SPSC queues are wait-free for both producer and consumer when they operate on separate threads. No mutexes, no contention, no blocking. boost::lockfree::spsc_queue is used throughout.

docs.title: Facade
docs.text:
What: Provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem. Hides internal wiring and lifecycle management from the caller.

Where:

  1. TradingEngine — constructs, wires, and manages the lifetime of all subsystems (NetworkIO, ParserDispatch, BuilderDispatch, OrderManager, RiskEngine, MarketBook, HashTables, SessionManager, LoginController, ClickhouseWriter). The caller only interacts with start() and stop().

Why: Without a facade, the caller would need to know the construction order, dependency graph, and thread lifecycle of every subsystem. TradingEngine encapsulates all of this.

docs.title: Strategy Pattern
docs.text:
What: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable at runtime or compile time.

Where:

  1. Builder_Dispatch — selects the appropriate builder (Builder_FIX, Builder_OUCH_BIST, Builder_OUCH_NASDAQ) based on the order's venue and protocol at runtime.
  2. Parser_Dispatch — routes incoming packets to the correct parser (Parser_FIX, Parser_OUCH_BIST, Parser_ITCH_BIST, etc.) based on protocol and venue.

Why: New venues or protocols can be added by implementing a new builder/parser and registering it in the dispatch — existing code is unchanged. Open/Closed Principle in practice.

docs.title: Chain of Responsibility
docs.text:
What: Pass a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides to process it or pass it further.

Where: RiskEngine::check_risk() — an incoming order passes through a sequence of independent checks:

  1. check_venue_halt_and_circuit()
  2. check_order_rate_limit()
  3. check_price_tick_valid()
  4. check_quantity_bounds()
  5. check_max_open_orders_account/symbol()
  6. check_self_trade_order()
  7. check_account_risk() (which itself chains: leverage, drawdown, unrealized loss, margin, balance, notional)

Each check returns a reject reason bitmask. The chain short-circuits on certain critical failures.

Why: Each risk check is independent, testable, and can be added or removed without touching others. The bitmask approach allows multiple reject reasons to be accumulated in a single pass.

docs.title: Command
docs.text:
What: Encapsulate a request as an object, allowing it to be passed, queued, stored, and processed independently of the requester.

Where:

  1. Order struct — every order (new, cancel, replace, fill) is represented as a self-contained Order object carrying all necessary state (venue, protocol, price, quantity, side, status, exec info). It is created once and flows through the entire pipeline — from strategy to risk to builder to network — without being reconstructed.

Why: Decouples the originator of an order from its execution. Each pipeline stage reads and writes the same Order object in place, avoiding copies and extra allocations.

docs.title: Composite
docs.text:
What: Treat a group of objects the same way as a single object. A composite object delegates to its children.

Where:

  1. Parser_Dispatch — owns and delegates to Parser_ITCH_BIST, Parser_ITCH_NASDAQ, Parser_OUCH_BIST, Parser_OUCH_NASDAQ, and holds a reference to Parser_FIX. A single parseFIX() or parseITCH() call dispatches to the correct child.
  2. Builder_Dispatch — owns Builder_OUCH_BIST, Builder_OUCH_NASDAQ, and holds a reference to Builder_FIX. A single build() call dispatches to the correct child.

Why: The rest of the system does not need to know which specific parser or builder handles a given message. The dispatch layer absorbs protocol and venue complexity.

docs.title: Factory Method
docs.text:
What: Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses or specific components decide which class to instantiate.

Where:

  1. LoginController::LoginAttempt() — constructs the correct login message (SBT Login or FIX Logon) depending on the session protocol.
  2. Builder_FIX / Builder_OUCH_BIST / Builder_OUCH_NASDAQ — each constructs a protocol-specific wire message from a generic Order object.

Why: The caller does not need to know the wire format of the message. It provides an Order and the factory produces the correct byte sequence for the target exchange.

docs.title: Observer (epoll)
docs.text:
What: Define a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified automatically.

Where:

  1. NetworkIO — epoll is the kernel-level implementation of the Observer pattern. Each socket file descriptor is registered as a subscriber (epoll_ctl), and epoll_wait() acts as the notification mechanism. When data arrives or a socket becomes writable, the corresponding event handler is invoked.

Why: Kernel bypass solutions (DPDK, RDMA, Solarflare OpenOnload) were not available due to hardware limitations. epoll was chosen as the most performant alternative available on standard Linux — it scales to thousands of file descriptors with O(1) event delivery, avoids busy-polling CPU waste, and integrates naturally with non-blocking sockets. Edge-triggered mode (EPOLLET) is used throughout to minimize spurious wakeups and syscall overhead.

docs.text: This page documents architectural explorations, design pattern evaluations, and optimization candidates benchmarked during the development.

docs.title: Exp-1 — Parser Dispatch and Protocol Parsers: Function Pointer Table (fptr) vs. Switch-Case
Overview
docs.text:
Message type dispatching across all binary and text protocol parsers (Mixed traffic, ITCH BIST, ITCH NASDAQ, and OUCH BIST) was evaluated to compare the performance trade-offs between static branch-based routing (switch-case) and indirect function pointer (fptr) dispatch.

Note: Both implementations run on the identical SPSC pipeline (boost::lockfree queue), ensuring queue-induced cache metrics remain baseline-equivalent.

Branch Misses 50.66M Higher branch variance Switch structures introduce heavier branch predictor strain across diverse message IDs. docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Result: While both architectures share identical inter-thread queue overheads, static switch-case routing causes measurable performance degradation (~8.6% to ~36.8% higher p50 cycles across micro-benchmarks and ~5% higher total CPU user time in full pipeline perf runs), alongside severe tail latency spikes (p999 up to +41%).
  • Why it was rejected: Large switch-case blocks over frequent message type discriminators increase branch misprediction penalties and instruction cache pressure in hot loops. Function pointers (fptr) provide clean, predictable, and isolated execution routing without bloating the dispatch block.
  • Outcome: Switch-case dispatch is rejected across the board; fptr routing remains in production.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The core order book data structure within the standalone MarketBook component was evaluated to compare performance trade-offs between cache-friendly B-Tree node indexing (absl::btree) and contiguous flat-array storage (std::vector).

Tests were conducted across realistic market replay workloads (64 symbols, up to 500 depth per side) under identical pipeline environments.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Result: std::vector causes severe performance degradation in mixed order book operations (median latency +89.5% slower, p99 tail latency ~7x higher) and inflates order book heap memory footprint by ~18x (35.37 MB vs 1.97 MB).

  • Why std::vector was rejected: Maintaining sorted array invariants forces $O(N)$ linear memory shifts (memmove) on every order book update. Under deep book depths, this produces massive instruction bloat (229.6B vs 81.9B instructions retired) and pollutes L1 Data Caches. High hardware IPC in vector is an artifact of raw memory copying rather than productive business logic.

  • Outcome: std::vector is rejected for production MarketBook usage; absl::btree remains in production.

docs.title: Recent Optimization
docs.text: The optimizations on this page were identified through profiling and benchmarking runs conducted against the baseline implementation. Perf results highlighted the bottlenecks; the changes below are the direct response to those findings.

docs.title: Opt-1 — OrderManager:: folly::ConcurrentHashMap → ConcurrentFixedFlatMap (2026-06-03)
docs.text:
folly::ConcurrentHashMap was replaced with a custom mmap-backed, fixed-capacity, open-addressing ConcurrentFixedFlatMap. The map is accessed exclusively by the store thread — concurrent access never occurs — making folly's hazard pointer and mutex machinery pure overhead.

Additionally, folly is not a modular library: even when only ConcurrentHashMap was used, the entire library was pulled into every build. Removing it cut full build time by ~2x.

docs.title: Benchmark Comparison (BM_OrderManager/MixedTraffic)
docs.text:
Metric Before (folly) After (ConcurrentFixedFlatMap) Δ Mean latency 2584 ns 2621 ns +1.4% (within noise) p50 cycles 7,261 7,736 +6.5% p95 cycles 7,941 8,643 +8.8% p99 cycles 8,903 9,471 +6.4% p999 cycles 183,912 17,400 −91%

Mean and steady-state cycle counts are effectively unchanged — the hot path cost of the map swap is neutral. The significant gain is in tail latency: p999 dropped −91%, directly attributable to the elimination of folly's hazard pointer reclamation and deferred free paths that caused occasional long stalls.

docs.title: Test Philosophy
docs.text: Each component is tested both in isolation and as part of the full pipeline. This allows measuring the cost of each stage independently before observing end-to-end behavior.

docs.title: Dataset Types
docs.text: Label Description Best Single-message/single-packet, ideal conditions Normal Full-messages/single-packet, realistic scenario Worst Partial-message(s)/multi-packet, stress conditions

docs.title: Test Structure
docs.text:
Five levels of testing were applied across all components:

  • Unit (gtest) — Correctness testing of each component in isolation
  • Benchmark (google benchmark) — Latency and cycle count measurement
  • Perf — Cache miss, branch prediction, TLB analysis...
  • AddressSanitizer (ASan) — Memory leaks, out-of-bounds accesses, and use-after-free bugs (minor leaks were successfully identified and resolved).
  • ThreadSanitizer (TSan) — Data races and deadlocks, ensuring strict thread safety across concurrent components (executed with clean runs).

docs.title: Component Hierarchy
docs.text: Where applicable, both the top-level interface and the underlying protocol handlers are tested independently. This isolates per-stage costs before measuring combined overhead — for example, measuring a FIX parser in isolation before measuring it through the parser dispatch layer.

docs.title: Builder Dispatch — Mixed Traffic
docs.text:
The dispatch benchmark reflects realistic production traffic — build requests from all protocols and venues are interleaved and processed through a single builder dispatch thread. The dataset contains FIX, OUCH BIST, and OUCH NASDAQ orders of varying types processed in sequence.

Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Mixed Traffic 262 (0.93%) 664 (0.10%) 814 (0.91%) 985 (114.47%)

3 orders per iteration (1 per protocol × 3 protocols). Average cost per order: 221 cycles (664 / 3).

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
• Single — a single new order processed in isolation; covers the minimal build path for that protocol.
  • Mixed — a sequence of varying order types processed in order: new order, replace, modify, cancel, and additional new orders. Reflects realistic production traffic where different order operations arrive in sequence.

docs.text: Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Single 175 (0.10%) 440 (0.00%) 498 (0.27%) 583 (5.10%)

docs.title: Builder Summary — Cost Breakdown
docs.text:
Mixed traffic dataset contains one FIX, one OUCH BIST, and one OUCH NASDAQ new order — all three processed per iteration.

Stage cycles FIX build — Single 440 OUCH BIST build — Single 30 OUCH NASDAQ build — Single 32 Total build cost 502 Builder dispatch full pipeline 664 Dispatch overhead 162 Build % of total 75.6% Dispatch overhead % 24.4% Dispatch overhead per order (3 orders/iter) 54 cycles (8.1%)

Notes: Build cost accounts for ~76% of total dispatch cost — the inverse of the parser where dispatch overhead dominates at 73–99%. This means the builder's optimization target is FIX serialization itself, not the dispatch path.

FIX message construction involves field-by-field ASCII encoding — a known cost of the protocol. At 440 cycles, FIX costs ~15x more than OUCH binary formats at 30–32 cycles. For high-order-rate scenarios, FIX serialization is the primary bottleneck in the build path.

OUCH binary formats at ~30 cycles each reflect the minimal cost of fixed-length struct serialization with no field encoding overhead.

docs.text:
• Single — a single message processed in isolation; covers the minimal order manager path for that message type.
  • Flow — a sequence of related messages processed in order; for example FIX: NewOrder followed by ExecutionReport and Cancel. Reflects realistic message flow through the order manager.
  • Mixed Traffic — 3 messages per protocol interleaved in random order across all protocols and venues. Reflects realistic production traffic patterns where messages from different protocols arrive concurrently.

docs.text:
The dispatch benchmark processes a mixed sequence of messages from all protocols and venues through the order manager in a single thread.

Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Mixed Traffic 2570 (3.51%) 7067 (4.07%) 8585 (7.67%) 178638 (8.72%)

15 messages per iteration (3 per protocol × 5 protocols). Average cost per message: 471 cycles (7067 / 15).

docs.title: Order Manager Summary — Notes
docs.text:
OUCH p999 anomaly. OUCH BIST and OUCH NQ show p999 values of 59k–80k cycles against p50 values of 210–326 cycles — a 200–380x ratio. FIX and ITCH p999/p50 ratios stay under 2x. OUCH order manager handles acknowledgement matching against a pending order table; occasional hash table probe depth variance or cache miss on the awaiting-ack lookup is the suspected cause of these tail spikes — not yet isolated. This warrants a dedicated follow-up test with hash table access instrumented separately.

ITCH single is faster than FIX single. ITCH messages carry market data that follows a simpler order manager path — no awaiting-ack table lookup required. FIX single at 120 cycles includes the full ack-matching path.

Flow cost is roughly 2x single across all protocols. Flow scenarios include both a new order and an execution report in sequence. The near-linear scaling confirms the order manager processes each message atomically in arrival order with no batching or reordering — minimal shared state overhead between consecutive messages.

docs.title: Parser Dispatch — Mixed Traffic
docs.text:
The dispatch benchmark reflects realistic production traffic — raw network packets from all protocols and venues are interleaved and processed through a single parser dispatch thread. The dataset contains both single-packet and partial (multi-packet) messages across FIX, OUCH BIST, OUCH NASDAQ, ITCH BIST, and ITCH NASDAQ.

Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Mixed Traffic 1585 (0.41%) 4413 (0.39%) 5426 (0.64%) 11204 (1.74%)

13 packets per iteration (variable per protocol × 5 protocols). Average cost per packet: 339 cycles (4413 / 13).

To isolate the contribution of the SPSC queue push, the same benchmark was re-run with queue push disabled:

Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Mixed Traffic (no queue push) 901 (1.07%) 2510 (1.17%) 2862 (2.01%) 5740 (0.61%)

Removing the queue push drops median latency from 1585 ns to 901 ns — a ~43% reduction — confirming that the SPSC queue push is the dominant cost in the dispatch path. This strengthens the case for replacing the current boost lockfree queue with a custom queue implementation tailored to this pipeline's access pattern.

docs.title: FIX Parser
docs.text:
The FIX parser layer consists of three measurable stages:

  • ParserFIX — top-level class; receives raw packets, calls nextFixMsg() to extract messages, dispatches parsed structs to the Order Manager queue.
  • nextFixMsg() — extracts a single FIX message boundary from a raw byte buffer; handles partial and multi-message packets.
  • parse() — constructs the message struct from a complete FIX message boundary.

docs.title: FIX Summary — Cost Breakdown
docs.text:
Using Normal and Worst (seq in-order) scenarios. parse() cost is taken as the average of NewOrder and ExecReport.

Stage Normal cycles Worst cycles nextFixMsg() 118 160 parse() avg 130 130 nextFixMsg + parse 248 290 ParserFIX full pipeline 924 1075 Dispatch overhead 676 785 nextFixMsg % of total 12.8% 14.9% parse % of total 14.1% 12.1% Dispatch overhead % 73.1% 73.0%

Dispatch overhead includes queue push to Order Manager, protocol routing, and buffer management.

Notes: Dispatch overhead accounts for ~73% of total pipeline cost in both scenarios — parse() and nextFixMsg() together represent under 30%. Queue push cost is therefore the primary optimization target for FIX parser latency reduction.

The seq out-of-order scenario costs slightly less than seq in-order despite higher complexity; with partial packets spread across non-contiguous boundaries, fewer messages complete per iteration, reducing queue push frequency.

p999 CV is elevated across all FIX scenarios — with only 10 repetitions, a single outlier disproportionately inflates tail percentiles. Production-grade tail measurement requires a minimum of 100 repetitions for stable p999 values. p50 CV stays below 2%, confirming hot path stability.

To investigate whether batching queue pushes could reduce contention, an additional variant was benchmarked: all messages in a packet are parsed first, then pushed to the queue in a single batch operation rather than one push per message.

docs.title: ParserITCH NASDAQ — Batch Queue Push
docs.text:
Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Best (single msg) 154 (1.84%) 318 (3.09%) 349 (3.54%) 426 (12.56%) Worst (multi-msg, single pkt) 226 (0.17%) 526 (0.00%) 722 (0.46%) 843 (5.22%)

The worst-case scenario drops from 307 ns to 226 ns (~26% reduction), confirming that batching reduces queue contention when multiple messages arrive in a single packet. The best-case result is unchanged, as a single-message packet already issues only one push.

Despite the improvement, batch push is not used in the current production path. Accumulating messages before the push introduces a handoff delay between pipeline units — downstream components receive nothing until the full packet is processed, which may create bottlenecks under real stress conditions that microbenchmarks do not capture. The current approach of parse-and-push per message is retained for now; this will be re-evaluated with further real-load stress testing prior to production deployment.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
• Update Single — a single market data message updates the risk profile; covers the minimal update path.
  • Update Flow — a sequence of related market messages processed in order: AddOrder followed by Execution and Cancel. Reflects a complete order lifecycle update.
  • Check Single — a single new order passes through risk validation before being forwarded to the next pipeline stage for exchange submission.

docs.title: Risk Check
docs.text: Scenario Median (ns) p50 cycles p99 cycles p999 cycles Single 131 (1.34%) 214 (0.30%) 342 (0.82%) 390 (2.65%)

docs.title: Risk Summary — Notes
docs.text:
Risk Update is the lightest component in the pipeline. Single update completes in 50 cycles — the lowest p50 across all benchmarked components. This is expected: update is a targeted write to a pre-allocated pool with no lookup overhead. Flow at 90 cycles covers a full order lifecycle update with minimal overhead increase, suggesting efficient state management with no significant contention between consecutive updates.

Risk Check costs ~4x more than Risk Update. Check at 214 cycles vs Update at 50 cycles. Check validates position limits and order constraints against the current risk state — a read-heavy operation involving multiple field comparisons. An open question for production sizing: is 214 cycles on an E-core within the acceptable latency budget for the check path? This depends on the order submission rate and acceptable risk gate overhead.

Part of the gap may also reflect the core assignment difference: Update runs on a P-core while Check runs on an E-core, which has lower single-thread throughput. See Threading Model for core assignment details.

Risk Update and Risk Check run on separate cores by design. Update is write-heavy and runs on a P-core. Check is read-heavy and runs on an E-core. Placing them on the same core would cause L1/L2 cache contention — writes from Update would invalidate cache lines read by Check.

docs.title: Builder — Perf Analysis
docs.text:
End-to-end profiling of the Builder unit across four test scenarios: Builder Dispatch (mixed protocol traffic through the dispatch layer), Builder FIX (FIX protocol message construction in isolation), Builder OUCH BIST (OUCH BIST venue message construction in isolation), and Builder OUCH NASDAQ (OUCH NASDAQ venue message construction in isolation).

The Dispatch test is the primary production-representative scenario. The protocol-specific tests isolate per-path contribution and confirm per-format characteristics without cross-protocol interference. The isolated tests exercise a narrow, single-message dataset and complete quickly — their value is in per-function branch/cache behavior, not in absolute throughput figures.

All scenarios are compute-bound and contention-free — zero HITM across the board, negligible LLC pressure, and L1-D miss rates well below 0.1%. The Builder unit's working set (Order structs, output buffers, dispatch table) fits comfortably in L1 across all paths.

FIX carries the highest IPC in isolation (3.52) with all data L1-resident. The OUCH scenarios show slightly lower IPC (2.75–2.87); branch miss at 0.01% and L1-D miss at 0.06–0.08% confirm the OUCH build loops execute cleanly. The two actionable findings (checksum accumulation and timestamp syscall) are FIX-path specific and are isolated in findings 2 and 3 of the Dispatch section.

docs.text: Overhead is the inclusive cost of a function and all its callees. Self is the cost of the function's own instructions only — the actionable signal.

IPC at 3.52 on P-core confirms FIX building is compute-bound with good throughput. docs.title: Findings & Action Items
docs.text:
Builder FIX isolates the pure FIX build path and confirms the findings from Dispatch:

  • IPC 3.52 confirms FIX building is compute-bound and well-optimised at the field-formatting level.
  • finalizeChecksum at 11.00% CPU self (vs 9.45% in Dispatch) — in isolation the full checksum loop cost is proportionally larger with no routing overhead diluting it. See Dispatch finding 2.
  • transact_time + epoch_to_transact_time at 9.66% CPU self (vs 7.63% in Dispatch) — localtime_r syscall path is the dominant timestamp cost. See Dispatch finding 3.
  • L1-D miss rate of 0.03% confirms the FIX buffer and Order struct fit in L1. No data working set concern.
  • iTLB at 272,287 confirms localtime_r kernel text as the primary iTLB stressor on the FIX path — consistent with Dispatch finding 3.

docs.title: OrderManager — Perf Analysis
docs.text:
End-to-end profiling of the OrderManager unit across six test scenarios: OrderManager (mixed protocol/venue traffic through the full store path), OrderManager FIX (BIST FIX message lifecycle in isolation), OrderManager ITCH BIST (BIST ITCH market data processing in isolation), OrderManager ITCH NASDAQ (NASDAQ ITCH market data processing in isolation), OrderManager OUCH BIST (BIST OUCH execution reports in isolation), and OrderManager OUCH NASDAQ (NASDAQ OUCH execution reports in isolation).

The Dispatch test is the primary production-representative scenario — it exercises the full store() dispatch path across all protocol and venue branches with a 17-message mixed dataset covering FIX, ITCH, and OUCH traffic for both BIST and NASDAQ. The isolated protocol tests each exercise a narrow 3–4 message sequence and are used to attribute per-path costs without cross-protocol interference.

The OrderManager is a deliberately broad orchestration component. It manages order lifecycle across multiple venues, maintains order pools, hash-based lookup maps, pending order tracking, MarketBook updates, and fan-out to downstream risk, strategy, and database queues — all within a strictly single-threaded store loop. The class comment explicitly notes that cache-line level micro-optimisation was intentionally deferred pending profiling; the results below constitute that first profiling baseline.

The 17-message dataset covers: instrument directory (BIST + NASDAQ), FIX new/partial/cancel (BIST), BIST ITCH add/exec/cancel, NASDAQ ITCH add/exec/delete, BIST OUCH accepted/executed/cancelled, NASDAQ OUCH accepted/executed/cancelled. Field Value Wall time 13.63 s User time 54.46 s Sys time 0.02 s CPUs utilized 3.996

Four threads active: the store thread (main, CPU 6) and three consumer spin-loops. User time at 54.46s across ~4 CPUs and 13.63s wall time is consistent with all four threads fully loaded for the run duration. IPC at 0.35 on P-core is memory-bound and spin-wait dominated. The store thread interleaves hash map lookups, order pool writes, variant dispatch, and five downstream queue pushes per message — all against a large, cross-thread-contested working set. The E-core IPC at 1.23 is higher than P-core despite doing less application work: the consumer spin loops (which land on E-cores as the OS migrates threads) consist of tight _mm_pause() + branch sequences that retire cheaply, inflating E-core IPC relative to the heavier store-path work on the P-core.

Branch miss rate at 1.00% is elevated relative to the isolated ITCH tests (0.00%) and reflects the std::visit / variant dispatch across the 17-message type mix. Each store() call dispatches through nested std::visit chains covering up to 14 BIST ITCH + 11 NASDAQ ITCH + 5 BIST OUCH + 11 NASDAQ OUCH + FIX message alternatives. The misprediction rate is not an application defect — it is inherent to the branch-per-variant-arm dispatch pattern across diverse message sequences.

L1-D miss rate at 3.48% reflects the combined pressure of the large order pool and hash map working set plus cross-thread cache line invalidation from the three consumer threads reading the same Order* pointers written by the store thread to the downstream queues. The LLC miss rate at 0.00% confirms the full working set is LLC-resident — the misses are L1-evictions caused by contention, not true capacity pressure.

Overhead Self Symbol 83.72% 2.81% OrderManager::store() 16.99% 11.02% folly::ConcurrentHashMap::eraseImpl 14.66% 1.21% OrderManager::update_order(FIXMessage*) 13.91% 4.75% std::__do_visit — NASDAQ ITCH 13.18% 13.13% HashTables::wyhash_small 10.40% 1.20% std::__do_visit — NASDAQ OUCH 8.74% 7.56% std::__gen_vtable_impl — BIST ITCH dispatch 7.64% 0.49% OrderManager::add_awaitingAck_order 7.39% 7.34% absl::flat_hash_map::find 6.74% 1.01% folly::ConcurrentHashMap::emplace 5.29% 2.21% OrderManager::add_market_order 5.13% 5.11% pthread_mutex_lock

HashTables::wyhash_small at 13.13% icache self is the largest single instruction footprint in application code. This is the hash function called on FIX execution report ID hashing. It appears on the hot path for every FIX exec report processed through update_order(FIXMessage*).

folly::ConcurrentHashMap::eraseImpl at 11.02% icache self is the most notable cost attributable to the awaitingAck_orders_ map. On every OUCH accepted/executed and FIX execution report, awaitingAck_orders_.erase(client_order_id) is called to remove the matched pending order. The eraseImpl footprint reflects folly's hazard-pointer-based reclamation machinery — each erase triggers a hazard pointer acquisition, bucket traversal, node unlink, and deferred reclamation enqueue. This is a structural cost of using a concurrent hash map on a path that is single-threaded in practice (the store loop never races with a writer on awaitingAck_orders_ except through add_awaitingAck_order, which is also called from the same store thread in the test). The use of folly::ConcurrentHashMap for awaitingAck_orders_ is the primary icache overhead item on the OUCH and FIX paths.

absl::flat_hash_map::find at 7.34% icache self is the order lookup cost on the market and our-order maps. With market_orders_ and our_orders_ both using absl::flat_hash_map<OrderKey, Order*>, each ITCH and OUCH message that requires an existing order lookup calls this function. The flat hash map has excellent cache characteristics (open addressing, linear probing), so this is expected and not a concern.

pthread_mutex_lock at 5.11% icache self is folly's internal mutex used by ConcurrentHashMap during bucket modification. This confirms that ConcurrentHashMap's internal locking contributes meaningfully to the icache footprint even on the single-threaded store path — hazard pointer operations and mutex acquisition are invoked on every insert/erase regardless of actual concurrent access.

The L1-I miss count at 372M is the highest across all OrderManager scenarios and reflects the diverse instruction footprint of the full dispatch path: six update_order overloads, five filler classes, two hash map implementations, and the folly hazard pointer machinery all contribute unique instruction pages. Metric Value Total shared cache lines 19 Load HITs on shared lines 112,642 Local HITM 45,310 LLC hits on shared lines 81,851 Locked accesses on shared lines 1 Blocked accesses on shared lines 1,653 Store HITs on shared lines 83,941

45,310 Local HITM across 19 shared cache lines is the dominant cross-thread contention signal. The 19 shared lines correspond to the SPSC queue ring buffer slots and metadata (head/tail pointers) written by the store thread and read by each of the three consumer spin loops. With three consumers each spinning on separate queues (store_to_risk, store_to_strategy, store_to_db), each queue write by the store thread causes an ownership transfer (HITM) as the relevant consumer reads the updated slot. This is structurally equivalent to the pipeline SPSC HITM and is a test harness artifact — in production, the consumer threads are doing meaningful work rather than busy-spinning.

No application struct false sharing is detected. The single locked access is a folly ConcurrentHashMap mutex acquisition, not a structural contention point.

Single-threaded in practice, slightly faster than ITCH BIST (0.57s vs 0.68s wall). The higher IPC (3.78 vs 2.63) suggests the NASDAQ ITCH sequence has a more compact execution profile — discussed below.

docs.title: Results (OrderManager OUCH BIST)
docs.text:
BIST OUCH execution report processing in isolation — bist_acc, bist_execO, bist_canO pushed per iteration, 5M iterations. One awaiting-ack order added per iteration via add_awaitingAck_order. Three consumer threads active. The OUCH path is the first scenario where awaitingAck_orders_ (folly ConcurrentHashMap) is fully exercised on every iteration — insert on ack-add, lookup on accept, erase on cancel/exec.

Field Value Wall time 2.70 s User time 10.61 s Sys time 0.01 s CPUs utilized 3.936

Four threads active — same structure as Dispatch. Wall time at 2.70s for 5M iterations (vs 0.68s for ITCH BIST at the same N) immediately signals that the OUCH path is ~4× slower per iteration than the ITCH path.

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text:
Metric P-Core E-Core Note Instructions 18.72B 9.64B E-core: significant spin consumer activity Cycles 44.06B @ 4.15 GHz 9.28B @ 0.87 GHz P-core near boost; E-core spin-wait clock IPC 0.42 1.04 P-core memory/contention-bound Branch miss rate 0.94% 3.18% P-core elevated — OUCH variant dispatch L1-D miss rate 3.03% — Elevated — folly hazptr + SPSC contention LLC miss rate 0.01% 15.22% P-core: LLC-resident; E-core startup noise

IPC at 0.42 on P-core is structurally similar to Dispatch (0.35) and OUCH NASDAQ (0.35) — the spin consumer threads and folly ConcurrentHashMap overhead together depress the observed IPC regardless of the actual store-path work. The OUCH processing itself is heavier than ITCH (map insert + hazptr emplace + map lookup + hazptr erase on every accepted message) which compounds the IPC depression.

L1-D miss rate at 3.03% reflects both cross-thread SPSC invalidation and the folly hazard pointer table accesses (hazard pointer slots are shared across threads, generating additional cache line bouncing on every ConcurrentHashMap operation).

L1-I misses at 3.99M is dramatically elevated relative to ITCH BIST (252K). This 16× increase is attributable almost entirely to the folly hazard pointer machinery — hazptr_domain::push_list, hazptr_inline_executor_add, hazptr_obj_cohort::reclaim_list — which brings in multiple instruction pages on every ConcurrentHashMap insert and erase.

docs.text:
Overhead Self Symbol ~75% ~25% each Three consumer spin lambdas 15.18% 2.57% OrderManager::store() 6.27% 6.19% BIST OUCH cancelled message handler lambda 4.77% 4.77% boost::lockfree::ringbuffer_base::push (SPSC) 3.18% 0.83% folly::ConcurrentHashMap::eraseImpl 2.30% 2.30% boost::lockfree::ringbuffer_base<Order*>::push 2.17% 0.07% OrderManager::add_awaitingAck_order 2.04% 0.19% folly::ConcurrentHashMap::emplace 1.77% 1.77% pthread_mutex_lock

The BIST OUCH cancelled message handler at 6.19% CPU self is the largest application leaf in this profile. The cancelled handler (OUCHOrderCancelledMessage) is the most complex OUCH response: it calls get_order_from_our_map (hash map lookup by OrderKey), fill_ouch_cancelled, and pushes to three downstream queues plus the db queue. Its prominence as a leaf — no further callee cost attributed to it — confirms the cancel processing instructions are dense and in-lined.

folly::ConcurrentHashMap::eraseImpl at 0.83% CPU self and emplace at 0.19% appear modest in the CPU+Branch profile but are the dominant icache contributors (see below) — the hazard pointer overhead is instruction-count heavy but not instruction-retire heavy, causing it to show up more strongly in icache than CPU profiles.

pthread_mutex_lock at 1.77% self confirms folly's internal bucket mutex is being acquired on the store thread on every OUCH accepted/cancel processing. This is structurally unavoidable with ConcurrentHashMap regardless of actual concurrent access.

docs.text:
Overhead Self Symbol 46.13% 1.80% OrderManager::store() 37.92% 1.01% asm_sysvec_apic_timer_interrupt (kernel timer) 32.49% 3.54% folly::ConcurrentHashMap::eraseImpl 22.32% 1.00% folly::hazptr_domain::push_list 20.06% 0.16% folly::detail::hazptr_inline_executor_add

folly::ConcurrentHashMap::eraseImpl at 3.54% icache self combined with hazptr_domain::push_list (1.00%) and hazptr_inline_executor_add (0.16%) — together 4.70% of icache self — confirm that the folly hazard pointer reclamation machinery is the dominant instruction footprint cost on the OUCH path. Each eraseImpl call traverses the bucket list, unlinks the node, and enqueues it for deferred reclamation through the hazard pointer domain. The kernel timer interrupt at 1.01% icache self reflects the elevated timer interrupt rate at 2.70s wall time — not an application concern.

docs.text:

L1-I misses at 3.99M vs ITCH BIST's 252K is a 16× increase driven by the folly hazard pointer infrastructure. iTLB at 144K vs ITCH BIST's 2.2K (66×) confirms that the folly hazptr and reclamation code pages span multiple iTLB entries that are not cached between calls. The operator new / cfree calls within ConcurrentHashMap also contribute to dTLB pressure (102K vs ITCH BIST's 25K) through heap allocator metadata accesses.

docs.text:
Metric Value Total shared cache lines 11 Load HITs on shared lines 22,948 Local HITM 8,400 Blocked accesses on shared lines 275 Store HITs on shared lines 17,462

8,400 Local HITM across 11 shared cache lines. The 11 lines include the SPSC queue ring buffers (same as Dispatch) and additional lines within the ConcurrentHashMap internal structure — the hazard pointer table slots and the bucket lock words are written by the store thread during insert/erase and read by the folly background reclamation path (which may run on a different core). Unlike the Dispatch HITM which is purely SPSC hand-off, the OUCH HITM has a structural contribution from folly's internal state, making it partially non-test-harness in character.

Structurally equivalent to OUCH BIST but with the NASDAQ OUCH variant chain and the additional nq_ouch_refnum_ordkey_ map. The NASDAQ OUCH path is the most complex per-message: it requires awaitingAck_orders_ lookup, add_our_order (pool slot + our_orders_ insert + orderhistory push), nq_ouch_refnum_ordkey_ insert/erase, and sympack_symid_ lookup on replaced/non-accepted messages.

Field Value Wall time 3.44 s User time 13.59 s Sys time 0.01 s CPUs utilized 3.949

Four threads active. Wall time at 3.44s vs OUCH BIST's 2.70s — NASDAQ OUCH is ~27% slower per iteration, attributable to the additional nq_ouch_refnum_ordkey_ and sympack_symid_ map operations on the exec/cancel paths.

docs.title: Parser — Perf Analysis
docs.text: Profiling of the parser under sustained load across all supported protocols. The parser dispatch test runs all protocols concurrently through the full dispatch pipeline. Per-protocol tests isolate each parser individually to expose protocol-specific cache and branch behavior.

docs.title: Test Setup
docs.text:
All perf tests were conducted under Profile 1 — Performance/Idle. For the full profile comparison and selection rationale, see Pipeline Overview.

Field Value CPU 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13620H (10C/16T) P-core max 4900 MHz Kernel 6.17.0-29-generic x86_64 Governor performance NUMA Single node, 15714 MB total

docs.title: Protocol Comparison at a Glance
docs.text:
Before diving into individual results, the cross-protocol comparison reveals the most important structural difference in parser behavior.

Protocol P-core IPC L1-D miss L1-I misses Branch miss Local HITM Dispatch (all) 0.46 4.96% 12.3M 0.37% 16,880 FIX 1.01 2.90% 208K 0.28% 4,528 ITCH BIST 0.19 10.32% 44K 2.37% 2,243 ITCH NASDAQ 0.20 10.27% 54K 2.56% 2,860 OUCH BIST 0.18 11.36% 247K 1.59% 9,265 OUCH NASDAQ* 2.26 0.30% 5K 0.01% 0

*OUCH NASDAQ was profiled as an isolated parse function test (no dispatch pipeline) — see OUCH NASDAQ for context.

The dominant pattern: FIX is compute-bound (IPC 1.01) with moderate cache pressure. ITCH and OUCH are severely memory-bound (IPC 0.18–0.20) — their high L1-D miss rates are driven by SPSC queue cache line contention, not struct complexity — as confirmed by the OUCH NASDAQ isolation test (IPC 2.26, L1-D miss 0.30% with no queue). The dispatch overhead and boost queue contention compound this in the combined test.

docs.text:

P-core at 0.46 is stalling on memory — queue writes, struct pointer chasing. The bottleneck is not the parsing itself but the inter-thread data movement via boost queue.

L1-D miss at 4.96% is the combined effect of boost queue head/tail pointer writes and the high L1-D miss inherent to ITCH/OUCH message structs (10%+ in isolation). FIX's lower miss rate (2.90%) partially offsets this.

Two near-equal worker threads dominate — feeder pushing packets, consumer dispatching. dispatch() at 2.78% self confirms it is a thin dispatcher, not itself the bottleneck. The 9.72% self on main reflects test driver overhead.

docs.text:
Metric Value Note L1-D miss rate 4.96% Mixed — queue writes + ITCH/OUCH struct access LLC miss rate 0.03% Very low — working set in LLC L1-I misses 12.3M Moderate — dispatch table + multiple parse paths dTLB misses 1,452K Elevated — boost queue buffer spans many pages iTLB misses 176K Low

dTLB misses at 1.45M stand out — the boost spsc queue with 1024 capacity holds large RxPacket pointers and its internal buffer spans multiple pages. Each queue push/pop potentially crosses a page boundary, adding TLB pressure. This disappears in the without-push test (153K dTLB misses) — confirming the queue buffer as the source.

docs.title: False Sharing (C2C)
docs.text:
Metric Value Total shared cache lines 2,020 Local HITM 16,880 Blocked accesses on shared lines 4,701

16,880 HITM is the highest of all parser tests and driven entirely by boost queue internal state — consistent with the pipeline RxTx findings. The without-push test shows 4,072 HITM, confirming ~75% of HITM in the dispatch test is boost-sourced.

Optimization Candidate

boost::lockfree queue head/tail contention is the dominant false sharing source. A custom SPSC queue with explicit cache line separation would reduce HITM by ~75% based on the without-push comparison. Pre-production redesign candidate.

docs.title: Bonus — Queue Push Overhead
docs.text: Queue push removed from the parser dispatch test. All protocols still parse, but parsed messages are not pushed to the downstream queue. Isolates the pure parser dispatch cost from the queue transfer cost.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Metric With Queue Push Without Queue Push Delta Wall time 10.70 s 5.67 s 47% faster CPUs utilized 2.970 1.959 One fewer effective thread P-core IPC 0.46 1.12 2.4× improvement Branch miss rate 0.37% 0.07% 5× fewer misses L1-D miss rate 4.96% 1.88% 2.6× reduction LLC miss rate 0.03% 0.19% Higher — cold LLC without consumer L1-I misses 12.3M 4.1M 3× fewer dTLB misses 1,452K 154K 9.4× reduction iTLB misses 176K 349K Higher — see note Local HITM 16,880 4,072 4.1× reduction

Every memory metric improves dramatically when the queue is removed. The IPC improvement from 0.46 to 1.12 confirms the parse logic itself is not memory-bound — the queue push operation is responsible for the majority of cache and TLB pressure in the dispatch test.

dTLB reduction from 1.45M to 154K (9.4×) is the most dramatic delta. The boost spsc queue's large internal buffer (1024-element capacity) causes TLB misses on every push as it spans multiple pages. Without the push, data TLB accesses are limited to the packet buffers themselves.

Hotspot shift without push: dispatch() rises to 10.98% self and parseFIX to 8.27% self — previously hidden beneath queue push overhead, now visible. This confirms the queue push was masking parsing cost in the full test.

LLC miss rate rises slightly (0.03% → 0.19%) — without a downstream consumer thread keeping parsed data warm in LLC, eviction pressure increases marginally.

Optimization Candidate

The queue push operation dominates parser performance — not parsing itself. A custom SPSC queue with cache-line-aligned head/tail and smaller default capacity would reduce dTLB pressure significantly. Pre-production redesign should evaluate this alongside the boost::lockfree replacement identified in pipeline profiling.

docs.title: Bonus — Without FIX
docs.text: FIX protocol removed from the dispatch test. Only ITCH BIST, ITCH NASDAQ, OUCH BIST, and OUCH NASDAQ handled. Isolates the FIX contribution to the combined dispatch numbers.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Metric With FIX Without FIX Delta P-core IPC 0.46 0.18 2.6× worse without FIX L1-D miss rate 4.96% 9.17% 1.85× worse without FIX Branch miss rate 0.37% 1.38% 3.7× worse dTLB misses 1,452K 1,170K Slightly lower — fewer queue writes Local HITM 16,880 9,823 Lower — fewer total queues

Removing FIX makes the parser significantly worse in IPC and cache behavior — this is counterintuitive but explained by FIX's superior cache characteristics. FIX messages are compact, sequentially parsed, and cache-friendly (IPC 1.01 in isolation). When FIX is present in the combined test, its cache-friendly access patterns warm up LLC lines and improve overall throughput. Without FIX, only ITCH and OUCH remain — their high L1-D miss rates (10%+) and low IPC (0.18–0.20) dominate the combined result.

Note

The without-push dcache profile shows NetworkIO::SBTPacketHandler at 17.55% self time — absent in the with-push test. OUCH packet demultiplexing happens inside the network layer via SBT packet handler before queue push, meaning part of OUCH processing cost lives in NetworkIO rather than the parser. Without FIX in the mix, OUCH dominates and this network-side cost becomes visible. The true OUCH parse cost is therefore split across NetworkIO and Parser_Dispatch — isolating just the parse function (as done in the OUCH NASDAQ parseFunc test) gives the cleaner picture.

docs.text: Profiling of the risk engine under two isolated scenarios: risk update (write path — update_risk() processing incoming order acknowledgements) and risk check (read path — check_risk() validating orders before submission).

docs.title: Test Setup
docs.text:
All perf tests were conducted under Profile 1 — Performance/Idle. For the full profile comparison and selection rationale, see Pipeline Overview.

Field Value CPU 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13620H (10C/16T) P-core max 4900 MHz Kernel 6.17.0-29-generic x86_64 Governor performance NUMA Single node, 15714 MB total

docs.text:
Metric Risk Update Risk Check Wall time 0.385 s 0.192 s P-core IPC 2.13 5.47–5.51 Branch miss rate 0.01% 0.00–0.01% L1-D miss rate 0.24% 0.01% LLC miss rate ~0% (absolute) ~0% (absolute) Local HITM 0 0

Both paths are compute-bound in isolation — IPC well above 1.0 in both cases with negligible cache pressure. This confirms the finding from pipeline profiling: the risk engine itself is not the bottleneck; cross-thread queue contention and E-core clock limitations are.

Risk check in particular stands out with IPC 5.47–5.51 and L1-D miss rate 0.01% — the check path is executing at near-peak efficiency when there is no concurrent writer on the shared structs.

docs.title: Results — Risk Update
docs.text:
update_risk() processes order acknowledgements — updating SymbolRisk, AccountRisk, and OrderRisk fields on fill, partial fill, cancel, and new order events. The test drives 10M iterations with a 3-order mix (fixNew, fixPartial, fixCancel) through store_to_risk, with two consumer threads draining risk_to_builder and risk_to_strategy. Risk state is reset after each batch.

Field Value Wall time 0.385 s User time 0.381 s Sys time 0.004 s CPUs utilized 0.996

Single-threaded execution on the update path — CPUs at ~1.0 confirms no meaningful parallel worker is active. Sys time at 0.004s is negligible. The two consumer threads (risk_to_builder and risk_to_strategy) drain their queues with _mm_pause() spin loops on CPU 0 and CPU 2; they consume negligible resources as the queues are always empty from their perspective (the update loop runs to completion before they can see data).

docs.text:
Metric P-Core E-Core Note Instructions 3.96B 1.17B E-core activity is startup/linker overhead Cycles 1.86B @ 4.84 GHz 1.33B @ 3.47 GHz P-core near boost IPC 2.13 0.88 See note below Branch miss rate 0.01% 3.44% P-core excellent L1-D miss rate 0.24% — Excellent LLC miss rate 46.66% of 26,886 loads 18.61% of 2.89M See note below

IPC at 2.13 on P-core — update_risk is compute-bound in isolation. The atomic fetch operations on SymbolRisk and AccountRisk fields are the dominant instructions; with a hot working set the P-core executes efficiently through the update chain. The E-core at 0.88 IPC and 3.44% branch miss reflects startup initialization rather than steady-state behavior — the E-core sample window is only 0.18% of total samples.

The 46.66% LLC miss rate on the P-core is an artifact of the small LLC load count (26,886 absolute loads). At this low denominator, a handful of cold startup misses produce a high percentage. The absolute LLC miss count (12,546 events) is negligible relative to the 1.12B L1-D load count — the application working set is comfortably L1/LLC-resident. The L1-D miss rate at 0.24% is the correct signal, and it is excellent.

docs.title: Hotspot Analysis
docs.text:
Overhead Self Symbol Profile 89.59% 46.68% RiskEngine::update_risk() CPU+Branch 46.26% 46.26% RiskEngine::update_risk_for_protocol_fix(AccountRisk&, AccountLimit const&, Order&, OrderMetrics) CPU+Branch 96.89% 60.43% RiskEngine::update_risk() dcache 35.83% 35.03% RiskEngine::update_risk_for_protocol_fix(...) dcache

update_risk() at 46.68% CPU self and 60.43% dcache self is the clear hot function — it drives the update dispatch and carries the bulk of atomic write cost directly. update_risk_for_protocol_fix() at 46.26% CPU self and 35.03% dcache self is nearly as costly on the CPU dimension — FIX order acknowledgements trigger the full update path including pending_notional_scaled and open_orders_count updates on every event, and the function carries its full cost as a leaf (no further callees visible in the profile).

The near-parity in CPU self-time between update_risk (46.68%) and update_risk_for_protocol_fix (46.26%) indicates the dispatch overhead in update_risk and the field write cost in the protocol-specific path are roughly balanced. In the dcache profile the split shifts toward update_risk (60.43% vs 35.03%), suggesting the dispatch and branching logic in update_risk generates proportionally more data access events than the targeted atomic writes in the FIX path.

ICache profile — kernel page fault dominant

The ICache record is dominated by kernel page-fault frames (asm_exc_page_fault → __handle_mm_fault → do_anonymous_page chain), consistent with the other Builder tests in this run. update_risk() is visible at 15.90% overhead — confirming it is sampled but suppressed by the kernel noise. This is a test harness artifact.

TLB profile — very low sample count

The TLB record accumulated only ~33 samples at this test duration. The top entry is snprintf at 72.73% self — this is a logging or initialization call rather than steady-state update path behavior. The dTLB miss absolute count (42,252) is low in absolute terms and is consistent with startup and OS activity rather than the update loop itself. The TLB profile is not meaningful at this sample depth.

L1-D miss rate at 0.24% is excellent in isolation. The SymbolRisk and AccountRisk fields written by update_risk() are hot in L1 — they are written repeatedly on consecutive calls and stay resident. The elevated L1-I misses (381K) are attributable to kernel page-fault text pages, identical in character to the Builder Dispatch findings, not to the update logic itself.

The HITM events seen in pipeline profiling for update_risk() are entirely caused by the concurrent check_risk() thread reading the same struct fields — not by anything inherent to the update path itself.

docs.title: Results — Risk Check
docs.text:
check_risk() validates orders before submission — reading SymbolRisk, AccountRisk, SymbolMeta, and Limits fields to enforce position, notional, and rate limit constraints. The test drives 10M iterations with a single order (strategy_to_risk) per iteration, with two consumer threads draining risk_to_builder and risk_to_strategy. Risk state is reset after each call.

Field Value Wall time 0.192 s User time 0.189 s Sys time 0.003 s CPUs utilized 0.993

Single-threaded execution — CPUs at ~1.0. Sys time at 0.003s is negligible. The test completes in 0.192s wall time with 10M iterations — substantially faster than the update test (0.385s at the same N), consistent with the much higher IPC and lower data miss rate on the check path.

IPC at 5.47–5.51 on P-core is the highest observed across all risk and builder scenarios in this run. check_risk() is a read-only validation path — reading SymbolRisk, AccountRisk, and Limits fields with no atomic writes. With L1-D miss rate at 0.01%, all read targets are hot in cache; the branch predictor handles the limit check conditions at near-zero miss rate; and the instruction stream is dense and predictable. The P-core is executing at near its retirement ceiling.

The 48.16% LLC miss rate is again an artifact of the small LLC load count (26,350 loads). The absolute miss count (12,690 events) is negligible relative to the 1.27B L1-D load count. The working set is entirely L1-resident — the 0.01% L1-D miss rate confirms this directly.

docs.title: Cross-Scenario: Update vs Check
docs.text:
The comparison between isolated results reveals the clear performance asymmetry between the write and read paths.

Scenario IPC L1-D miss HITM Source Update isolated 2.13 0.24% 0 Clean Check isolated 5.47–5.51 0.01% 0 Clean Pipeline E-core (RxTx) 0.44 — ~14K (shared) Cross-thread contention

Check outperforms update by ~2.6× in IPC and 24× in L1-D miss rate in isolation. The update path performs atomic read-modify-write operations on multiple fields per order event — these are inherently more expensive than the pure reads of the check path, and their cost is correctly reflected in the IPC and miss rate gap even when no cross-thread contention is present.

The gap between isolated and pipeline performance is entirely explained by cross-thread interaction — concurrent readers and writers on the same SymbolRisk cache lines, E-core clock limitations, and boost queue contention. The risk engine implementation is efficient on both paths; the pipeline bottleneck is the runtime environment.

docs.title: Pipeline Benchmark Results
docs.text: End-to-end latency from network ingress to risk check completion, measured across four CPU frequency profiles and two load conditions. All values are medians with CV (coefficient of variation) shown in parentheses.

docs.title: Test Setup
docs.text:
Each benchmark,

  • receives a single new order acknowledgement packet through the complete Rx pipeline — from raw network bytes arriving on the socket, through protocol parsing, to risk update completion,

  • sends a single new order packet through the complete Tx pipeline — from risk checking to the packet being written to the network.

docs.title: Summary — Best Profile (Performance/idle) Across All Protocols
docs.text: Performance/idle (Profile 1) represents the ceiling: highest clock frequency, lowest system contention. The table below compares all five protocols under this single profile.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Why Performance/idle (Profile 1) wins despite CPU scaling enabled:

When C-states are active, threads do not all run at peak load simultaneously, so the CPU can boost individual cores to 4700 MHz. When idle is disabled (Profiles 3) all cores are held active at once, and the chip cannot sustain maximum frequency across all of them — settling around 3200 MHz under thermal/power constraints. The result is that idle-enabled runs achieve higher per-core clock rates even though the benchmark issued a scaling warning.

ITCH vs FIX/OUCH gap (~40% fewer cycles):

Not a parsing difference. ITCH carries market order data that does not affect our risk profiles, so the risk engine bypasses most of its update path for these messages. FIX and OUCH order acknowledgements trigger the full update.

CV elevation:

Occasional CV spikes — particularly at p99/p999 — are measurement artefacts rather than pipeline instability. With only 10 iterations, a single outlier sample disproportionately inflates the percentile. The p50 CV remains below 2% in almost all cases, confirming the hot path itself is stable.

Turbo vs no-turbo (Profile 4):

With turbo disabled, the CPU is capped at 2400 MHz regardless of load. Beyond the frequency penalty, turbo-off runs did not show better stability — p999 CV is comparable to or worse than turbo-on profiles. Given both the latency cost and the absence of a stability benefit, turbo-enabled is the preferred deployment configuration.

Both the network receive and transmit threads run simultaneously. This is the most representative scenario — it reflects real deployment load and exposes cross-thread contention that single-path tests cannot reveal.

Wall time is the real elapsed duration of the test. User time is the sum of CPU time spent in userspace across all threads — with ~7 threads running, 48s user over 7s wall is expected."Sys time (6.68s, ~12% of user) reflects kernel time spent on continuous socket maintenance and event loop (epoll) machinery on network layer; this is on the higher side and shows kernel bypass importance."

IPC at 0.46 reflects the pipeline's architecture, not a problem. A compute-bound workload runs 2.0–4.0 IPC on modern cores. docs.text: Overhead is the inclusive cost of a function and all its callees — high overhead on a dispatcher is expected. Self is the cost of the function's own instructions only — this is the actionable signal. High self time means the function itself is consuming CPU, not delegating to children.

P-core hosts all flow threads — OrderFlow, RiskFlow, BuilderFlow, ParserFlow all appear at 13–16% self time, load is evenly distributed. NetworkIO::recv_send() acts as a dispatcher at 0.40% self. The syscall chain (entry_SYSCALL_64 → sendto) descends from 13.5% to 4.6% — this is the source of the icache miss pressure observed in the icache profile. epoll_wait at 1.33% self is expected.

Optimization Candidates

RiskEngine::check_risk() — 10.88% E-core self time. check_risk was intentionally placed on an E-core given its read-heavy profile. However at 10.88% self time and given the 36% clock frequency gap between E-core (3600 MHz max) and P-core (4900 MHz max), this placement has a measurable latency cost on the order path. Pre-production thread affinity redesign and hardware limit analysis should revisit this assignment.

L1-I misses are elevated at 2.05B — roughly 12× the L1-D miss count. The icache record confirms this is syscall-driven, not application code size. The top samples from the icache profile are shown in the raw output; __x64_sys_sendto and __sys_sendto appear at ~50%, directly attributing the pressure to the Tx sendto path. Each syscall entry drags kernel text into the icache and pollutes the iTLB, which explains the 700K iTLB miss count.

Metric Value Total shared cache lines 3,724 Load HITs on shared lines 39,792 Local HITM 14,392 Locked accesses on shared lines 2,637 Blocked accesses on shared lines 3,023

14,392 Local HITM events are present, but detailed cache line analysis shows no application struct false sharing. The majority of HITM originates from boost::lockfree queue internal head/tail state. Remaining events are test-only artifacts absent in production. See C2C details.

Optimization Candidate

The dominant false sharing source is boost::lockfree queue state shared between RiskFlow and OrderFlow threads. A custom SPSC queue with explicit head/tail cache line separation would eliminate this. Pre-production redesign should evaluate replacing boost::lockfree with a purpose-built queue.

docs.text:
Receive path only — no transmit thread running. Used to isolate the Rx contribution to RxTx numbers and verify path-specific behavior without cross-path contention.

Field Value vs RxTx Wall time 6.60 s ~6% shorter — no Tx thread competing User time 45.84 s Expected: ~1 thread fewer Sys time 6.16 s ~8% lower — sampling variance CPUs utilized 7.881 Near-identical to RxTx

The Rx-only sys time (6.16s) establishes a nearly identical baseline to the RxTx-heavy scenarios, confirming that the kernel footprint is dominated by the active socket connections maintained with the simulator. Since the overhead persists even without the internal engine's Tx path, it proves that the kernel-space context switching and socket state management—driven by the fake server's traffic—accounts for the bulk of the sys time, rather than the Tx processing logic itself."

Structure mirrors RxTx P-core exactly — same dispatcher pattern, same self-time distribution. NetworkIO::recv_send() at 0.43% self is consistent with RxTx (0.40%). The absence of BuilderFlow and ParserFlow in the top 10 here is a sampling artifact from the shorter symbol list, not a structural change; OrderFlow at 13.67% self confirms the thread load is equivalent.

RiskEngine::check_risk() drops from 10.88% self (RxTx) to 8.99% in Rx-only. In Rx-only the Tx thread is absent — no orders are submitted, so check_risk() spins idle with no work to validate. The reduced self time reflects the lower call rate from zero outgoing order flow, not a change in per-call cost. The 36% E-core clock gap concern from RxTx remains valid regardless — frequency is fixed, only call volume changes.

docs.text:
Metric Value vs RxTx L1-D miss rate (P-core) 0.96% Matches RxTx — Rx owns the data working set LLC miss rate (P-core) 0.11% Half of RxTx (0.22%) — Tx working set removed LLC miss rate (E-core) 0.08% Slightly higher than RxTx (0.05%) — sampling variance L1-I misses (P-core) 1.91B 7% lower than RxTx — fewer syscalls dTLB misses (P-core) 179K Lower than RxTx (249K) — Tx buffer allocations absent iTLB misses (P-core) 1.16M Higher than RxTx (700K) — see note

iTLB misses at 1.16M in Rx-only vs 700K in RxTx is counterintuitive. With fewer syscalls the iTLB should be under less pressure. The likely explanation is sampling normalization: in RxTx the iTLB miss events are distributed across more active threads and wall time is slightly longer, diluting the per-run count. The icache profile confirms the syscall chain is still the dominant iTLB stressor in Rx-only.

docs.text:
Metric Value vs RxTx Total shared cache lines 335 91% fewer than RxTx (3,724) Load HITs on shared lines 2,254 94% fewer Local HITM 772 95% fewer than RxTx (14,392) Locked accesses on shared lines 151 94% fewer

HITM collapses from 14,392 to 772 in Rx-only. The same boost::lockfree queues are active in both scenarios, but Rx-only HITM per queue is 11–17x lower than RxTx. With only the Rx path running, producer-consumer timing naturally staggers and queue pointer contention rarely materializes. Adding the Tx path in RxTx creates simultaneous bidirectional pressure on the same queues, amplifying contention sharply. boost::lockfree performs well under single-path load — the contention is a cross-path interaction effect, not a boost-specific deficiency. A custom queue with explicit cache line separation would eliminate the residual contention regardless.

Rx-only surfaces no independent optimization candidates. All findings from RxTx hold and the Rx path contributes cleanly:

  • LLC miss rate in isolation (0.11%) confirms the Rx working set is well-contained — the 0.22% in RxTx is Tx-driven.
  • False sharing in Rx-only is negligible (772 HITM) — the boost::lockfree contention identified in RxTx is a cross-path artifact, not an Rx-internal issue.

docs.title: Results (Tx)
docs.text:
Transmit path only — no receive thread running. Used to isolate the Tx contribution to RxTx numbers. Tx is the dominant source of syscall pressure, icache pollution, LLC contention, and false sharing in the combined run.

Field Value vs RxTx Wall time 6.57 s ~7% shorter User time 44.54 s Expected: ~1 thread fewer Sys time 6.72 s Near-identical to RxTx (6.68s) — see note CPUs utilized 7.804 Near-identical to RxTx

Sys time in Tx-only (6.72s) matches RxTx (6.68s) almost exactly, which primarily reflects the heavy network overhead generated by our local fake server—acting as a test artifact—to simulate exchange traffic. Since the Rx-only sys time (6.16s) is also similar, this confirms that the overall kernel footprint is dominated by the active socket connections and baseline epoll machinery sustained between our engine and the simulator, rather than the internal routing of the Rx path itself.

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text:
Metric P-Core E-Core vs RxTx IPC 0.46 0.45 Identical Branch miss rate 0.14% 0.06% Slightly lower — Tx path has simpler branching than Rx parse L1-D miss rate 0.63% — Lower than RxTx (0.97%) — see note LLC miss rate 0.41% 0.03% P-core higher than RxTx (0.22%) — see note L1-I misses (P-core) 2.23B — Higher than RxTx (2.05B) — Tx is the dominant icache stressor

L1-D miss rate drops to 0.63% in Tx-only vs 0.97% in RxTx. The Rx parse path (packet struct reads, ring buffer writes) is the heavier L1-D consumer. Tx without Rx has a narrower data working set — packet build and send buffer access — which fits more comfortably in L1.

LLC miss rate rises to 0.41% in Tx-only vs 0.22% in RxTx. This is the most surprising inversion. In RxTx the Rx working set is hot in LLC from continuous use; removing Rx leaves the LLC colder between Tx accesses, increasing miss rate. The Tx send buffers and packet structs are accessed at high frequency but without the Rx path warming adjacent LLC lines, eviction pressure increases.

L1-I misses at 2.23B in Tx-only exceed RxTx (2.05B). Tx is confirmed as the dominant icache stressor. The icache profile shows __tcp_transmit_skb appearing at 58.5% overhead — a symbol absent from the RxTx and Rx profiles — indicating TCP stack traversal on the send path contributes meaningfully to kernel text pressure beyond sendto alone.

dTLB misses at 60K vs RxTx 249K — the largest relative delta across all metrics. The Rx path (packet struct population, ring buffer slot mapping) generates the majority of data TLB pressure in the combined run. Tx alone touches a narrow, stable set of data addresses.

iTLB at 1.28M vs 700K in RxTx mirrors the L1-I pattern — Tx syscall stream alone generates more iTLB pressure than the combined run's average, because in RxTx the Rx thread's non-syscall samples dilute the iTLB miss rate.

docs.text:
Metric Value vs RxTx Total shared cache lines 1,179 68% fewer than RxTx (3,724) Load HITs on shared lines 18,927 52% fewer Local HITM 5,669 39% of RxTx total (14,392) Locked accesses on shared lines 1,514 43% fewer

Tx-only produces 5,669 HITM — 39% of the RxTx total. Combined with Rx-only's 772 HITM, cross-path interaction in RxTx generates the remaining ~8,000 HITM beyond what either path produces in isolation. In Tx-only the dominant HITM sources shift — test artifacts (BuilderFlow/main lambda interaction, FakeTCPServer) and kernel network stack spin locks lead the cache line table, with boost::lockfree contributing at index 4 (104 HITM) via the NetworkFlow→Builder queue. The boost RiskFlow/OrderFlow contention that dominates RxTx is absent here because without the Rx parse path feeding orders, that queue sees minimal bidirectional pressure.

Tx-only's 1,179 shared cache lines vs RxTx's 3,724 confirms that RxTx contention is not simply additive — the cross-path interaction creates contention on lines that neither path stresses alone.

docs.title: Findings & Action Items
docs.text:
Tx-only confirms and sharpens the RxTx findings. No new optimization candidates emerge, but causality is clearer:

  • Sys time equivalence (Rx=6.16s ≈ Tx=6.72s ≈ RxTx=6.68s) proves the syscall budget is not directly related to Rx or Tx paths themselves.
  • L1-I miss leadership (Tx=2.23B > RxTx=2.05B > Rx=1.91B) confirms Tx as the icache stressor. __tcp_transmit_skb appearing in the Tx icache profile but not in RxTx or Rx indicates the TCP stack traversal is a secondary contributor alongside sendto.
  • HITM at 5,669 in Tx-only, 772 in Rx-only, 14,392 in RxTx: the ~8K gap is interaction-driven. The boost::lockfree replacement identified in RxTx findings eliminates the root cause regardless of which path is active.
  • LLC miss inversion (Tx=0.41% > RxTx=0.22%) is expected behavior — not a regression, an isolation artifact. In production the combined working set keeps LLC warmer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Unit tests for Builder_Dispatch — the component responsible for routing outbound orders to the correct protocol builder (FIX, OUCH BIST, OUCH NASDAQ), constructing wire-format TxPackets, and pushing them to the sender queue.

Tests are written with Google Test (gtest). The test pushes Order* objects directly to the risk_to_builder queue and verifies the resulting TxPacket bytes and metadata.

docs.title: BuilderDispatchTest.MixedMessageTraffic

docs.text:
• Each order is dispatched individually — risk_to_builder.push() followed by builder_dispatch->dispatch() — to verify that routing and building are correct per call without batching effects.
  • Socket index assignment (sock_index 0, 1, 2) maps directly to the session order registered in SessionManager — FIX BIST, OUCH BIST, OUCH NASDAQ respectively.
